title: Java Encapsulation
learningObjectives: Define encapsulation as bundling data with controlled operations.
Use private fields to restrict direct external access.
Create getters and setters for controlled field access.
Validate proposed state changes before updating an object.
Explain how encapsulation protects class invariants.

understand.concept: Encapsulation keeps an object's data and the operations that manage it together while controlling access to internal state. A common approach is to declare fields private and provide public methods that validate or expose appropriate values.
understand.whyItMatters: Encapsulation prevents callers from placing an object into an invalid state. It also allows the class implementation to change while keeping its public methods stable.
understand.analogy: Think of a well-designed object as a small service with a clear responsibility: it keeps the information it owns and exposes only the operations other code needs.
understand.analogyLimit: This analogy is only a design aid; Java access, inheritance and dispatch follow the language's exact rules.

explain.narrative:
## Private state

Declare fields private so other classes cannot read or change them directly. This makes the class responsible for protecting its own state.

## Getters and setters

A getter returns an allowed view of a field. A setter can validate an incoming value before changing the field. Not every field needs both methods; expose only the operations the class should support.

## Maintain invariants

An invariant is a rule that should remain true for every valid object, such as a non-negative account balance. Validate updates at the class boundary.

## Common mistakes

- Creating setters for every field without considering invariants.
- Returning mutable internal collections without protection.
- Confusing encapsulation with simply generating getters and setters.

examples.title: Read a private field through a getter
examples.code:
class Member { private String name = "Ravi"; public String getName() { return name; } }
public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) { System.out.println(new Member().getName()); } }
examples.explanation: The getter provides controlled read access.

examples.title: Validate a setter
examples.code:
class Temperature { private int celsius; public boolean setCelsius(int value) { if (value < -273) return false; celsius = value; return true; } public int getCelsius() { return celsius; } }
public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) { Temperature t = new Temperature(); t.setCelsius(25); System.out.println(t.getCelsius()); } }
examples.explanation: The setter checks the proposed value before changing state.

examples.title: Reject invalid state
examples.code:
class Wallet { private int amount; public boolean deposit(int value) { if (value <= 0) return false; amount += value; return true; } public int getAmount() { return amount; } }
public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) { Wallet w = new Wallet(); w.deposit(-5); System.out.println(w.getAmount()); } }
examples.explanation: A non-positive deposit is rejected and the balance remains valid.

examples.title: Expose a read-only field
examples.code:
class Product { private final String code = "P-10"; public String getCode() { return code; } }
public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) { System.out.println(new Product().getCode()); } }
examples.explanation: A getter can expose a value without providing a setter.

examples.title: Use methods to update state
examples.code:
class Counter { private int value; public void increment() { value++; } public int getValue() { return value; } }
public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) { Counter c = new Counter(); c.increment(); c.increment(); System.out.println(c.getValue()); } }
examples.explanation: Callers request a valid operation rather than changing the field directly.

practise.guidedTask: Create a small Java program about java encapsulation. Predict its output, then compile and run it with JDK 21.
practise.independentTask: Build an original program demonstrating java encapsulation in a practical scenario. Include at least two test cases, expected outputs and a short explanation of your design choices.
hints: Identify the class, object or type that owns each piece of state or behaviour.
Trace the declared type and runtime object separately when inheritance is involved.
Compile after each small change and compare actual output with your prediction.
practise.challenge: Extend one java encapsulation example with a realistic boundary case and explain how the design handles it.

questions.prompt: Which modifier commonly hides an object's fields?

questions.prompt: What is a setter commonly used for?
questions.answer: To validate and update a field

questions.prompt: Must every private field have both a getter and setter?
